newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Amsterdam to Asia July air cargo active, rates up.
newsitem.headline: Amsterdam to Asia July air cargo active, rates up.

text.p: Amsterdam cargo carriers are reporting that July freight capacity is being filled and rates are increasing to Asia though those to the Middle East rates are mixed, Reuter survey showed.
The Asian market contrasts with the expected seasonal slow-down in July when passenger traffic often dominates.
Two destinations singled out for special mention this month are the Indian sub-continent and Australia/New Zealand.

Though happy with the freight activity this month, last Friday's proposal by Schiphol of a nighttime ban on noisier wide-body jets has been the single issue dominating industry talk this week at Schiphol and elsewhere.

KLM Royal Dutch Airlines, Martinair, Polar Air and El Al may be the worst hit by the proposal, but other carriers are worried about its effect on Schiphol's bid to become a leading cargo airport. Three 747-200F operated by Atlas Air on behalf of KLM will also be hit.
Israel Chervin, El Al's cargo manager, said business between the Netherlands and Israel is healthy but that a move of the carrier's cargo operations may be necessary following this ban.
It will be impossible to change many of the schedules because they are largely dictated by the perishable industry in Israel, said Chervin.

Flowers are picked and processed during the day in Israel and the flights leave at around 2000 local(1800 gmt)and arrive at Schiphol around midnight, he said. The aircraft then leave for Israel in the proposed banned hours.

As carriers mull over the implications of the night ban, busy activity in the market continues to assure booked cargo space. Rates to Asian destinations have all seen increases, though those to the Middle East are mixed.
An Air Lanka cargo spokesman said space on the airline's three-times-week Airbus A340 aircraft is hard to come by, with capacity full.
The carrier is the sole operator between Amsterdam and Colombo and the spokesman said livestock, one day old chicks, ships spares and machinery are major exports to Sri Lanka.

A spokesman from Air Cargo Trader, general sales agent for Emirates airline is the Netherlands, said that business to the United Arab Emirates had not seen the drop-off in business that the company expected for this time of the year.
"It was the same at Christmas and the New Year, the cargo is still out there despite the holiday season."
Cargo from Italy, France and Germany goes ex-Netherlands on an Atlas Air Boeing 747-200 freighter that Emirates shares with KLM Cargo on the route.
But cargo from the Netherlands has not dipped as much as cargo from these countries he said, perhaps because those countries have more of a definite factory closure period in the vacation period.
Exports to Dubai include machinery, ships spares, vegetables and computer equipment, he added.
The Atlas freighter which Emirates shares with KLM calls at Schiphol three times a week to Dubai and travels on to Hong Kong once a week.
Herman Eikema, cargo manager of Air India, described the Dutch-India market as 'booming'. The Indian carrier operates once weekly with a Boeing 747 Combi aicraft.
"Flights are absolutely full with anything from electrical goods, spare parts, machinery to flower bulbs."

Bulbs are being exported to India, then the flowers are grown there and re-exported back into the Netherlands. This relatively-new industry is growing, he added. Textiles and leather goods are major exports from India.
July is very busy but he admitted, there may be a slow-down in August when the holiday-season really kicks-in.

Rates to India have shown significant increases and there are signs that they may continue to rise, with moves by the major carriers to India, Air India, KLM and Lufthansa, to increase them over the last few months.
The fuel surcharge did help to keep rates at a higher level as many carriers absorbed the rise rather than reducing rates again.
Rates can now reach up to three Dutch guilder level to India per kilogram.
Dick Plas, manager of Air Agencies, a general sales agent of ten airlines in the Netherlands, said that his clients will not be effected by the Schiphol night-ban.
But he added that he is worried about the issue as to where this leaves Schiphol as a major freight centre.
Air New Zealand, Plas said, an offline carrier in the Netherlands, has a lot of potential as there is currently much interest in the region, with cargo doing well.
Air Agencies also represents Biman Bangladesh Airlines which also offers a great deal of potential. The carrier operates from Brussels to Dhaka.
Hong Kong-carrier, Cathay Pacific cargo manager Achim van de Graaff, said flights leaving Amsterdam are full, with Australia and Japan especially performing well.
Machinery, electronic equipment including photocopiers are some of the exports to Australia. The Australian demand is boosting exports to the country, he said.
Hong Kong is still very stable and has not shown any significant increase since the handover to the Chinese.
North Asian destinations Korean and Japan are currently strong destinations.
Japan especially, is getting even more hectic as the flower bulb season is set to begin again in early August.
Nippon Cargo Airlines marketing manager Tatsuya Katayama, said NCA's three-times-weekly Boeing 747-200 freighter will be affected by the new Schphol night ban in winter time.
He reported that Japan is very busy, despite the summer season.
Cathay Pacific gets involved in the Japanese bulb season which lasts until late-September time. Daffodils and tulips are special favourites in Japan.
Rates to Hong Kong have increased by three to four percent last month, said van der Graaff.
Taiwan too, is extremely busy for the time of year.

A China Airlines cargo spokesman said the Dutch-Taiwanese market is doing very well, so much so that the airline is considering adding a second frequency by the end of the year with the arrival of a Boeing 747-400 aircraft.
But he admitted that the increasing restrictions may make the airline look twice at expanding the operation at Schiphol.

Thai Airways International's five times a week MD-11 flights to Bangkok are experiencing healthy freight bookings in July, its cargo spokesman said, with anything from spare parts to chemicals being exported to Thailand.
